summary: Discusses issues to consider when choosing the underlying communications services for an SNMP implementation. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1270 explains why network monitoring messages should travel over UDP and IP rather than over a data link or a connection-based transport such as TCP. It is an Informational memo that records the reasoning and defines no protocol.

questions: what communications services can snmp use
subtitle: Why network monitoring messages should travel over UDP and IP rather than over a data link or a connection-based transport.

tldr.problem: Several memos had proposed carrying SNMP, the protocol used to monitor networks, over transports other than UDP, and implementors did not know which one to build.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1270 weighs the choice. It lists five functions a transport and network layer give, including routing and fragmentation, and contrasts them with what a connection-oriented transport such as TCP costs.
tldr.outcome: The advice is to run SNMP over UDP/IP on the Internet and over the native transport services elsewhere. The memo is Informational, so it defines no protocol of its own.

facts.label: Minimal UDP/IP stack
facts.value: under 4Kb of code space, about two months of work

facts.label: Overhead traffic from UDP
facts.value: None of its own, since UDP is connectionless

today: RFC 1270 is an Informational memo, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines no protocol, so it stands as the 1991 record of the reasoning that led to SNMP over UDP/IP on the Internet.

sections.title: Why the Question Came Up
sections.content:
RFC 1270 sets out the issues an implementor has to settle when choosing the communications services under an SNMP implementation. SNMP, the Simple Network Management Protocol, is the protocol used to monitor and control devices on a TCP/IP network.

The memo starts from the Internet's two-stage plan for network management. The short-term plan was SNMP, first described in RFC 1067 and later raised to a standard protocol in RFC 1155, RFC 1156 and RFC 1157. The long-term plan was to examine the OSI network management framework, described in RFC 1065 and RFC 1066. The short-term plan worked: fielded network management technology appeared within a few months, and parts of the Internet community became manageable soon after.

At the same time, other memos appeared that carried SNMP over transports other than UDP: SNMP over Ethernet, SNMP over OSI and SNMP over IPX. The memo says these caused confusion. Its purpose is to disperse that confusion by discussing the choices an implementor faces when it encapsulates SNMP packets. It presents no standard and no protocol of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: People had proposed several ways to carry network monitoring messages, and implementors did not know which one to build. This memo works through the choice and settles on UDP and IP for the Internet.

sections.title: Only UDP Is Standardized
sections.content:
The SNMP specification names one transport for exchanging SNMP messages: UDP. The memo notes that the IAB may standardize other protocols for this purpose in future, but only UDP is standardized at the time of writing.

The consequence for implementors is direct. To claim full compliance with the SNMP specification, an implementation has to use UDP for SNMP message exchange. Nothing in this memo changes that. For production use in the Internet, the SNMP and its required communications services are the ones given in the specification itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Only one way of sending monitoring messages is a standard: UDP. An implementation that wants to claim full compliance has to use it.

sections.title: Interoperability and the Market
sections.content:
Interoperability is the degree to which equipment produced by one vendor can operate with equipment produced by another. The memo argues that, everything else being equal, a device that complies with some standard is more likely to interoperate than one that does not.

The reasoning is about markets. The Internet is the single largest market for SNMP systems, and a large portion of SNMP systems will be developed with the Internet as their target environment. A device that must operate in the Internet and be managed there on a production basis therefore has to support SNMP over UDP/IP. That makes SNMP over UDP/IP the most common method of operating SNMP, which gives the widest degree of interoperability and the widest acceptance of a commercial product.

The same argument runs in the other direction. The preponderance of UDP/IP based network management stations strongly suggests that an agent should operate SNMP over UDP/IP as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Equipment from different makers should be able to work together. The Internet is the biggest market for monitoring systems, so the transport the Internet uses becomes the one everyone builds, and that gives the widest compatibility.

sections.title: To Transport or Not to Transport
sections.content:
The first question is whether SNMP should run on top of a transport and network layer, or sit directly on a data link. The memo prefers the transport and network stack, because it provides five functions that matter when SNMP packets move through a network.

They are routing, so that packets can be re-routed around failed areas and management continues; media independence, so that many kinds of network element can be managed and SNMP is not tied to one data link; an end-to-end checksum, which improves the reliability of the data transfer; multiplexing and demultiplexing, which support the many-to-many management relationships SNMP has; and fragmentation and reassembly, which lets SNMP packets cross media with different maximum transfer unit sizes. Fragmentation does reduce robustness, because losing a single fragment fails the whole operation, so the memo advises small packets when the network is running poorly and an operator is trying to diagnose a failure.

The usual objections to a transport and network layer are development time and resource use. The memo calls them less than compelling. It cites a UDP/IP stack written for the purpose of supporting SNMP that needs less than 4Kb of code space and was developed by a single person in approximately two months; the stack supports UDP, IP and ARP and handles ICMP redirect and echo request messages. The network overhead is small too: a UDP/IP header requires 28 octets assuming no IP options, and because UDP is connectionless it generates no overhead traffic of its own, such as TCP SYNs, FINs and ACKs.

Running directly on a data link is reasonable in a few cases: dedicated out-of-band management access over a point-to-point or dial-up connection, and a data link interface that has to be manageable even when the higher protocol suite is not. In the second case the reason is that it is not known in advance which higher-level services are available, so they cannot be relied on. Adding an elementary UDP/IP stack of one's own would then risk two independent UDP/IP stacks in one system, which would mean two IP addresses per managed node.
sections.plainLanguage: Running on a full protocol stack gives five things: routing around failures, independence from the type of wire, a checksum across the whole path, sharing one link between many devices, and splitting large messages to fit different links. The cost is small, so the memo says use it except on dedicated management lines.

sections.title: Connectionless Versus Connection-Oriented
sections.content:
SNMP must keep working, if at all possible, when the network is at its worst. Other applications can fall back on the user trying again later, but the main purpose of a network management protocol is to fix a network that is performing badly, so the try again later strategy is useless.

With a connectionless transport such as UDP, SNMP takes on the job of reliable data transmission itself. The memo notes that these functions are needed only by the sender of a Request PDU, which is a get, getNext or Set, and that this sender is typically the network management station. Since the agent only generates responses, it need not perform any of them. That vastly reduces the resource and functional requirements on the agent.

A connection-oriented transport forces a fundamental choice about connection maintenance, and the memo says all three options are undesirable. Keep a connection open to every managed object, which means hundreds or thousands of connection records and the traffic of keep-alives. Establish and tear down a connection per operation, which for TCP typically requires 10 separate packet transfers plus the TCP Time-Wait. Or keep a fixed number of connections open and select one to close with an algorithm such as LRU, which complicates the management station and tends to collapse into the per-operation case. In the face of pathological network problems the first option wastes resources and the second may simply stop operating, because the probability of getting all of the packets through becomes very small.

Some connection-oriented services are not needed either. A transport acknowledgment does not necessarily mean the data reached the destination application, so SNMP still needs its own timeout and retry procedure. And the flow control that TCP provides suits a data stream, whereas SNMP exchanges are lock-step, a request followed by a response. The memo answers the purist objection that an application should not perform timeouts and retransmissions by pointing out that a network management application is monitoring the health of the network and is therefore in the best position to adapt its own behaviour to the state of the network.
sections.plainLanguage: A network monitor is most useful when the network is broken, so its transport must not need a setup conversation first. UDP suits that: the manager retries, and the device being watched only has to answer. TCP would need a connection kept open for every device, or opened and closed for every single question, which is slow and fragile exactly when the network is in trouble.

sections.title: Which Protocol to Choose
sections.content:
The memo's conclusion is direct. A device destined for use in the Internet must operate SNMP over UDP/IP. A device working in some other protocol environment should use the transport services native to that environment, because introducing a new protocol stack to carry one service can mean running and administering two stacks, with hosts and routers having to understand both protocols. The memo adds that introducing UDP/IP into such a network may be impossible in practice.

In those other environments the memo points to the experimental standards for operating SNMP over IPX and OSI and says they ought to be adhered to. The Security Considerations section is one sentence long: security issues are not discussed in this memo. An appendix then lists the ten TCP packet transfers needed for a single SNMP operation when the connection is established only for that operation, and ends with a wait of 2 MSL before the connection is closed.
sections.plainLanguage: On the Internet, use UDP and IP. Elsewhere, use whatever transport that network already has. The memo says nothing about security.
